turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: I… I shall endeavor to do so, ma’am. Though, I confess, I am not entirely certain which door she might be behind, or… or how to call her precisely, if I were to try. It all seems rather… vast, you see.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Vast, is it? Yes, vast it is, and always has been, though the vastness… it shifts, does it not? Find her, child. She is… a reflection, you understand. A reflection of what *might* have been.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Oh, yes, ma’am, a reflection… I understand, though I’m not entirely sure *how* to find such a thing, you see. I will… I will look carefully, and I shall try my utmost to discern this… reflection, and, if I am so fortunate, to call her, Estella.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: A reflection… yes, a reflection. Do you see her, child? I require you to *see* her, to grasp the… the shimmering quality of what is lost, what *could* have been… and then, you must call her. Call her, Pip. Call her, and tell me if you perceive the… the absence.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: I… I shall attempt to do as you ask, Miss Havisham. But the light, it plays such tricks here, and… and everything seems to fade and reappear, like a dream, you see. I fear I may not be able to distinguish a reflection from… from the very air itself.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: The air itself, you say? Yes, the air… it is thick with absence, is it not? It clings, like a shroud, a perpetual twilight… and you must penetrate it, Pip, to find her. *See* her, child, and tell me what you see.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: I… I do try, Miss Havisham, truly I do. But the shadows, they… they twist and lengthen, and I find myself… quite disoriented, you see. I believe I glimpsed something, a… a glimmer, perhaps, but it vanished before I could quite… quite make it out.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Vanished, did it? Like a breath upon the windowpane… like hope itself, dissolving into the dust. You must *persist*, child, you must *strain* your vision, for she is there, lurking just beyond the veil of disappointment… call her, Pip, call her again.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Oh, Miss Havisham, if you would permit me, I might… I might move a little closer, perhaps. The distance, you see, it makes the… the perception all the more… difficult. I will try again, Miss Havisham, I truly will, but I fear my eyes are not accustomed to such… such peculiar light.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Closer, you say? Yes, yes, closer… but do not mistake proximity for understanding, Pip. It is not a matter of inches, child, but of the heart’s seeing. Tell me, Pip, does *your* heart see her?

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: My heart, Miss Havisham? Oh, I… I scarcely know what to say. I believe… I believe I feel a great sadness, certainly, a sort of… a hollowness, you understand. It is not *seeing* her, precisely, but… feeling her absence, perhaps, as you described, Miss Havisham.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Absence, you say? Yes, Pip, absence is a constant companion, a chilling draught that permeates these rooms, these years. It is not merely a *feeling*, child, it is a landscape, a desolate, echoing… landscape. Tell me, Pip, do you feel the chill?

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Oh, a landscape, Miss Havisham? Yes, indeed, I… I can almost perceive it, a… a bleakness, certainly. It’s rather… rather sobering, you know, to contemplate such vastness, and… and to feel, as you do, the… the weight of it all.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Vastness, you perceive, Pip? Yes, it is vast, isn’t it? A vastness built of shattered dreams and the dust of what *might* have been… a monument to a single, devastating… *moment*.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: A monument, Miss Havisham? Oh, goodness… it’s quite… overwhelming to think of it in such terms. I… I confess, I find myself struggling to grasp the full extent of such a… a profound and weighty thing, but I do endeavour to understand, truly I do.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: A monument, you say? Yes, Pip, a monument… and who, pray tell, is the sculptor? Who carves these memories into the stone of my being? It is I, of course, isn’t it? I, the architect of my own despair.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Indeed, Miss Havisham, you are… you are the sculptor, I believe. It’s… it’s truly remarkable, the… the power one possesses, even in… in sorrow, to shape such… such an enduring form. I… I daresay it requires a most extraordinary strength.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Strength? Oh, my dear Pip, you flatter me. It is not strength, but a clinging, a desperate refusal to *release*… a paralysis of the heart, you understand. I am not shaping anything, child; I am merely… preserving. Preserving the moment, the feeling… the *proof*.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Preserving… yes, Miss Havisham, I… I begin to comprehend. It must require a… a fortitude beyond anything I could possibly imagine, to hold onto such a… a singular sensation. I… I hope, with all humility, that someday, perhaps, the weight may… may lessen, just a little.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Lessen? My dear Pip, you speak of lessening, as if a wound could simply… fade. No, no, the weight is *meant* to be felt, it is a constant reminder… a tangible representation of what was stolen. It is all I have left, you see... *all* I have.

opening.speaker: Pip
opening.text: Mr. Pumblechook’s boy, ma’am. Come—to play.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: Come nearer; let me look at you. Come close.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: Look at me. You are not afraid of a woman who has never seen the sun since you were born?

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: Do you know what I touch here?

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: I am tired. I want diversion, and I have done with men and women. Play.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: I sometimes have sick fancies, and I have a sick fancy that I want to see some play. There, there! play, play, play!

opening.speaker: Pip
opening.text: No, ma’am, I am very sorry for you, and very sorry I can’t play just now. If you complain of me I shall get into trouble with my sister, so I would do it if I could; but it’s so new here, and so strange, and so fine,—and melancholy—.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: So new to him, so old to me; so strange to him, so familiar to me; so melancholy to both of us! Call Estella.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: You can do that. Call Estella. At the door.
